title: Sewing & Weaving
intent: Threading, sewing and weaving are among the very best builders of the fine-motor control and hand strength writing will need.
Over-under weaving is early pattern and sequence made physical — a rhythm the hands and eyes learn together.
Slow, fiddly work builds real perseverance and the satisfaction of sticking with something hard.
Making a genuine object — a woven mat, a sewn picture, a threaded necklace — brings pride and purpose.
It's calming, absorbing, side-by-side work that invites quiet talk and helping one another.
implementation: Start where each child is — big threading beads, then a colander and pipe cleaners, then binca and blunt needles, then real weaving.
Model the rhythm slowly: 'Over... under... over... under... now pull it all the way through.'
Set up a permanent weaving frame (a fence, a hoop, a loom) children can add to over days and weeks.
Name the pattern and sequence as children work: 'You went over, under, over — that's the pattern.'
Encourage sticking with it: 'That bit was tricky and you kept going — look how much you've done.'
Offer rich, tempting materials — ribbons, wool, fabric strips, natural finds — to weave in.
Let children keep and display their work, and photograph the process to show how it grew.
key_questions: What comes next — over, or under?
How does the thread feel when you pull it all the way through?
What could you weave in next to change the pattern?
That was fiddly — how did you keep going?
What are you making, and who might it be for?

impact.text: Children thread, sew and weave with increasing fine-motor control, precision and hand strength.
Children follow and create an over-under sequence, building early pattern-making.
Children persevere through fiddly, demanding work and feel the satisfaction of finishing.
Children design and make a real object, choosing colours and materials with intent.
Children work calmly alongside others, talking about their work and helping one another.
Children talk about the sequence and their choices as they work.

enhancements: A weaving frame or loom set up on a fence, hoop or box that stays out over time.
Ribbons, wool, fabric strips, garden ties and natural finds to weave in.
Binca, hessian and blunt tapestry needles for sewing pictures.
Colanders, pegboards and pipe cleaners for early threading.
Large beads, pasta and buttons to thread into necklaces and patterns.
A display area and process photos showing how the weaving grew.

playing_exploring: Children explore how thread and materials behave as they pull, loop and weave.
They test different materials to weave in and see what happens.
active_learning: Children persist with slow, fiddly work and return to a long weaving over days.
creating_thinking: Children follow and invent patterns, plan what to make and choose their materials to match.
